_comment: GRAND over the whole of Peru, at 3 arc-seconds. A SURVEY, not a result of the same standing as the Arequipa full-DEM run: every physics criterion below is copied unchanged from grand_arequipa_full.json so the two are comparable, and everything that differs is a consequence of the grid. Read the area as a coarse national number and say so. There is no TAMBO counterpart to this file, deliberately -- see _comment_no_tambo.
_comment_criteria: Identical to grand_arequipa_full.json. The point of this run is scale, not a different question, and a criterion changed here would make the two incomparable.
_comment_size: Peru is roughly -18.4 to 0.0 lat and -81.4 to -68.6 lon: 18.4 by 12.8 degrees. At 3 arc-seconds that is 22,080 x 15,360 = 339 Mpx, and the pixel is 92.2 m N-S / 91.6 m E-W at the mid-latitude. At 1 arc-second it would be 3,052 Mpx, which is not a single run on this machine.
_comment_memory:
estimate_peak_memory_gb(22080, 15360, ds, stride) over the grid this run could use, in GiB:

        stride 10   stride 15   stride 30
  ds 1     12.36       10.39        8.42
  ds 2      7.86        5.89        3.92
  ds 4      6.74        4.77        2.80

Against ~7 GiB usable. downsample_factor 4 with candidate_stride 15 is 4.77 GiB, which leaves real headroom -- and headroom is the point: the estimator advertised 2.32 GiB for the full Arequipa DEM and that run peaked at 5.68 GiB before being recalibrated (ROADMAP 6.26a). ds 4 / stride 10 is 6.74 GiB, within 4% of the cap, and is the run to try second rather than first.
_comment_max_memory: 8.0, and it is squeezed between two constraints that pull opposite ways -- read both before changing it. (1) It is NOT the 4.77 GiB estimate plus a margin: estimate_peak_memory_gb estimates ANONYMOUS memory, deliberately excluding the memory-mapped DEM because the kernel can evict it, while max_memory_gb is applied as RLIMIT_AS, which caps VIRTUAL address space and so counts every mapping -- this DEM's 1.36 GB .npy cache, the two 339 MB ping-pong buffers, all of it. Measured: at 7.0 the whole search completed and then the map died with 'Unable to allocate 40.8 MiB', so the virtual high-water mark is just over 7.0. (2) But a cap ABOVE available memory is not a cap at all -- the OOM killer arrives before RLIMIT_AS fires. 11.0 ran to completion here and is the value that took the machine down on the next run, at candidate_stride 10. 8.0 clears the measured failure point with ~1 GiB to spare and stays under the ~8.7 GiB this machine has available. It is inferred from those two measured points rather than tested at exactly 8.0. If the two constraints cannot both be met on your machine, the configuration does not fit: raise candidate_stride, which is the memory lever, rather than raising this. Never 0 -- that disables the cap entirely. preflight_memory now warns when this exceeds available memory (ROADMAP 6.46).
_comment_gap_close: 1.5, not the 1.0 it would default to from antenna_spacing_km. Stride 15 on a 92.2 m pixel leaves a 1,382 m gap between kept candidates, and a closing element that cannot bridge it leaves the mask a scatter of isolated pixels -- the 4.75x under-report of ROADMAP 6.34. warn_stride_outruns_closing(15, 92.2, None, 1.0) warns at ratio 1.38; at 1.5 km it does not. The cost of raising it is the opposite error: an element 1.5x the array's own spacing will bridge some gaps that are real, so area is biased slightly high rather than catastrophically low. That is the right direction for a survey and it is declared here rather than discovered later.
_comment_rfi: none, not a preset. SETTLEMENT_PRESETS holds Arequipa and Lima only, and applying a regional list nationally would exclude towns in one department and none of the others -- worse than excluding nothing, because it looks like it was done. The right fix is a national settlement list from OpenStreetMap via oroscope-fetch-roads --places, which is a job of its own: an Overpass query over 1.3 million km2 is not one request.
_comment_no_tambo: There is deliberately no tambo_peru_survey.json. Two reasons, both about the grid rather than about Peru. First, a 90 m pixel cannot resolve the geometry TAMBO depends on: Colca's floor is ~1 km wide and its rim-to-rim separation ~4.5 km, so a canyon is ~11 pixels across at 3 arc-seconds and the wall the array stands on is a handful -- the 20-60 degree slope band would be measured on a wall that the grid has already averaged away. Second, TAMBO's 100 m antenna spacing sets a 100 m closing element against this run's 1,382 m stride gap, a ratio of 13.8; bringing gap_close_km up to 1.5 km to survive that is fifteen times the array's own scale, so the closed mask would smear across the canyon instead of tracing the wall and the area would be wrong in the opposite direction from ROADMAP 6.34. A national TAMBO answer needs 1 arc-second and tiling, and that is a different job.
_comment_origin: Deliberately null: read from the DEM's own ModelTiepointTag.
